<div class="note">
<span class="lab">What this produces</span>
<p>Collections in which named concepts are known to carry a phenotype contrast. With them: a
score for how much of that planting the estimator gave back, and a placement of concept-space
recovery between the best any method could reach and alignment at random.</p>
</div>

The modalities are measured on different individuals, so what connects them is a fixed vocabulary of
named biological concepts. A concept is a set of features that belong together for a stated
biological reason, and every modality is scored on the same concepts. A validation therefore has to
answer two questions that no real cohort can. Are the concepts that move with the phenotype the
ones that get called? And does a concept scored in one modality track the same concept scored in
another?

## What a simulation has to reproduce, and what it does not

The estimator reads a normalised feature-by-sample matrix. Fragment bias, retention time, ionisation
efficiency and isotope envelopes are modelled upstream of that matrix, and normalisation removes or
absorbs them before anything reaches the estimator. The simulation target is therefore not
measurement physics but the six properties of a prepared matrix the estimator can respond to:

1. the per-feature marginal distribution, including its skewness and tail weight;
2. the mean-variance relation across features;
3. missingness as a function of abundance;
4. the feature-feature correlation structure, summarised by its eigenspectrum;
5. non-Gaussianity relevant to the recovery of free dimensions;
6. the design margins, including unpopulated cells and covariates recorded in only one cohort.

A generator that reproduces these properties provides a useful observation-model stress test. Which
properties of a real assay it does not capture bounds what recovery on it establishes.

## Three questions, three constructions

| Construction | What is simulated | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| Planted concepts | Named concepts that carry the phenotype contrast in every modality that expresses them | Whether the concepts that take part get called, and whether the rest of the vocabulary stays quiet |
| Borrowed observation model | The same structure, read through the marginals, missingness, correlation and design cells of real layers | How recovery changes when the matrix has the shape of the data the method is applied to |
| Withheld pairing | Two modalities measured on the same individuals, encoded as though disjoint | Whether the identity the vocabulary asserts is the correspondence the pairing shows |

## Planting concepts

`chorale_concept_example()` builds a collection in which named concepts carry a phenotype shift.
The vocabulary, how many of its concepts are planted, how many features a modality measures of each,
and the size of the shift are all arguments.

```r
library(chorale)

fx <- chorale_concept_example(n_samples = 60, n_features = 200,
                              n_concepts = 6, n_planted = 2,
                              effect = 0.1, coverage = 1, seed = 1)
fit <- chorale_concept_fit(fx$containers, fx$sets, n_free = 0,
                           n_permutations = 999)
chorale_score_concepts(fit, fx$planted)$summary
```

`chorale_score_concepts()` answers two questions rather than one. **Recall** is the share of planted
concepts that were called. The **false positive rate** is the share of the rest of the vocabulary
that was called as well. A method that calls everything answers the first and fails the second, so
neither is the result on its own.

**Rank AUC** is the probability that a planted concept outranks one that was not planted. A
threshold is a choice and a ranking is not, so the ranking says how far the two are separated
whatever cut is applied. Chance is 0.5.

Which control decides a call is an argument, because the two answer different questions.
`criterion = "fdr"` holds the share of calls expected to be false at the configured level;
`criterion = "family_wise"` holds the probability of any false call anywhere in the vocabulary.

`chorale_plant()` plants concepts into the observation model of real layers instead. The planting
and scoring vocabularies are the same one, because a concept is planted and recovered by name: the
question is whether the design shows it changing with the phenotype, not whether its composition
can be rediscovered.

## Recovery curves

`chorale_validate_concepts()` runs a grid of regimes, draws several collections from each, and
averages the recovery over them. Three dials matter and each asks a different question.

```r
grid <- data.frame(label = c("0.20", "0.10", "0.05", "0.02", "0.00"),
                   effect = c(0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0),
                   n_concepts = 6L, n_planted = 2L,
                   n_features = 200L, n_samples = 40L)
chorale_validate_concepts(grid, n_rep = 5, n_permutations = 999)
#>   label effect recall false_positive_rate rank_auc n_evaluated
#> 1  0.20   0.20    1.0                0.05    1.000           5
#> 2  0.10   0.10    0.4                0.10    0.825           5
#> 3  0.05   0.05    0.1                0.00    0.675           5
#> 4  0.02   0.02    0.0                0.00    0.600           5
#> 5  0.00   0.00    0.0                0.00    0.550           5
```

Recall falls away between a per-feature shift of 0.2 and one of 0.05 standard deviations, in forty
samples per cohort with concepts of about thirty features. The false positive rate stays at or below
the level it was called at throughout, and at a shift of zero the ranking sits at chance, which is
what a calibrated null looks like from this side.

**Effect size** asks how strong a concept's phenotype contrast has to be. The unit is
the shift in each member feature, not in the concept score, and the difference matters. A concept
score is a mean over its members, so a shift of \(d\) in each of \(m\) members that are otherwise
independent moves the score by about \(d\sqrt{m}\). Concept scoring aggregates, which is why
per-feature effects far below the threshold of a per-feature test are recovered.

**Sample size** asks whether bulk cohorts are large enough. **Vocabulary coverage** asks how far the
vocabulary has to reach into a modality's measured features, which is the question an incomplete
annotation raises. A concept defined on fifty features but measured on twelve is scored on the
twelve.

A regime the estimator cannot be run in is reported with its reason rather than as an empty cell. A
coverage low enough that no concept reaches the minimum number of features leaves nothing to score,
and that is a result about the regime.

## Giving the simulation the shape of real data

`chorale_data_profile()` measures the six properties from any matrix and returns them as one object.
It stores summaries rather than data: no sample identifier enters it, and no covariate left
unnamed.

```r
profile <- chorale_data_profile(assay = my_matrix, col_data = my_design,
                                covariates = c("phenotype", "sex"),
                                layer = "PROT")
```

Passing the profile to `chorale_simulate()` replaces the observation model with it and leaves the
latent structure untouched. Each simulated feature is read through a real feature's quantile grid,
so the values that come out have the distribution a real feature had. The map is monotone, so the
sign and the ordering of a planted design response survive it. The design is drawn from the
cells the real cohort populated, so a cell no sample occupied stays empty.

Correlation enters separately, as directions drawn at random in feature space with Gaussian scores
whose variances follow the profile's eigenvalues, scaled until the leading direction carries the
share of variance the profile records. Those scores are Gaussian, so they add covariance without
adding anything a decomposition driven by non-Gaussianity could recover as a source.

`chorale_profile_agreement()` places a simulated matrix beside the real one on the same six
properties, which is what a claim of realism is bounded to.

## Recovery against a withheld pairing

Where two modalities were measured on the same individuals, the pairing can be withheld and used
afterwards. `chorale_destroy_pairing()` presents the two modalities under their own sample
identifiers, encodes them as though disjoint, and only then uses the pairing to ask whether a
concept scored in one tracks the same concept scored in the other.

```r
r <- chorale_destroy_pairing(paired_a, paired_b, design, sets = sets,
                             n_random = 200)
r$concept_summary
#>   n_concepts paired_upper_bound recovered_agreement random_baseline
#> 1          4             0.8827              0.8827          0.2713
#>   placement_between_bounds fraction_partner_correct
#> 1                        1                        1
```

Three quantities frame the result. The **paired upper bound** is the best alignment the pairing
admits, which is what any method knowing the pairing could reach. The **random baseline** is the
mean over one-to-one relabellings of the concepts drawn at random. The **recovered agreement** is
the identity the vocabulary asserts, concept for concept by name, computed without a paired sample
ever having been seen. A placement of 1 means the identity is the correspondence the pairing shows.

The agreement is a signed correlation, because a concept score has a fixed orientation. A larger
score means a larger weighted mean of the features carrying the concept, so two modalities that rank
the same state in opposite directions have not recovered it. Random alignment is therefore a
baseline and not a bound. A vocabulary whose names line up while the biology does not places below
it, and the placement reports that as a negative value rather than clipping it to zero.

Per-concept results say where that holds and where it does not.

```r
r$concept_recovery
#>   concept self_agreement best_partner best_agreement partner_correct
#> 1    beta         0.9764         beta         0.9764            TRUE
#> 2   alpha         0.9739        alpha         0.9739            TRUE
#> 3   gamma         0.9737        gamma         0.9737            TRUE
#> 4   delta         0.6067        delta         0.6067            TRUE
```

The benchmark takes any two modalities measured on the same individuals and any vocabulary, so it is
a property of the estimator rather than of one collection.

## Validating families and joint transfer

Concept recovery alone does not validate the newer group and joint analyses.
Their simulations need distinct targets.

For a concept family, plant modest concordant shifts across several overlapping
concepts and compare them with families whose members point in opposite
directions. Recovery means the concordant family statistic gains power while the
discordant sum cancels, with family-wise error controlled under a complete
null. Because the definitions overlap, every member must reuse the same signed
permutation draw; independent null draws would be an invalid benchmark.

For a joint state, plant a low-rank pattern over several concept columns in
every modality, then assess four properties separately:

1. reconstruction over observed entries;
2. loading stability across starts and sample perturbations;
3. calibrated phenotype evidence on the fitted scores; and
4. leave-one-modality-out prediction in a modality excluded from fitting.

The fourth is the strongest test of cross-modality portability. It still does
not prove a component is a unique latent mechanism: sign, order, and rotations
remain non-identifiable, and more than one low-rank basis can describe the same
reconstruction. Simulations should therefore compare loading subspaces or
matched directions, not raw component labels.

Coverage missing by modality must also be planted explicitly. Joint-state
selection currently uses a zero-filled matrix for reproducibility selection and
the observed-entry mask for fitting. A validation should vary that coverage
pattern so selection artefacts are not mistaken for biological rank.

## Conditions of applicability

Recovery measured under borrowed marginals holds for marginals resembling the profiled ones. A
modality whose distribution or missingness differs materially requires its own profile.

A concept reaches a modality only through the identifiers or classes that modality carries. A
lipidome resolves at the level of lipid class, not lipid species, and a metabolome with no class
mapping cannot be scored on a pathway vocabulary.

The effect size a curve is drawn against is a shift in each member feature. A concept score
aggregates its members, so the same curve read as though the unit were the concept score would
overstate what is being asked of the data by about the square root of the concept's size.

Correlation outside the planted concepts is reproduced as its eigenspectrum, through directions
drawn at random in feature space. Those directions carry no biological grouping, so a modality whose
dominant axis has a biological identity is reproduced in the share of variance that axis carries and
not in which features it uses.

Concept-space recovery measured against a withheld pairing is measured where a pairing exists.
Whether it holds in a collection assembled from separate deposits is what the pairing benchmark
bounds rather than what it establishes.
